rationale: A wins because it keeps the facts on a leash and turns the same update into four clean reporter shapes. Its best line, "Peloton would rather rent you a bike than sell you one," is a real business-model story with the right proof asks; B's comparable angle trips over "built itself on a $1,000+ hardware sale" and "becoming a subscription company," which are not supplied and not cleanly true. B has usable bones, but A is the one I would let near a reporter first.
gaps_in_A: "positive adjusted EBITDA and free cash flow for the first time in three years" overclaims the free-cash-flow history; the update only supports the first profitable-quarter claim and current positive FCF.
"first hard evidence the cost program worked" implies causality between the $200M cuts and adjusted profit before showing the mechanics.
"new-CEO first-year scorecards" assumes a CEO timeline the update does not provide.
gaps_in_B: "built itself on a $1,000+ hardware sale" invents a price point not in the update. Cheap garnish, expensive credibility hit.
"the hardware company is becoming a subscription company" is sloppy; Peloton already has memberships, and the supplied fact is rental expansion, not a total identity change.
"connected-fitness comeback story" and "once-doubted retention story" import a narrative the provided facts do not establish.
"the retention problem may be the one that's actually fixed" jumps from record-low churn to a solved problem. A reporter will make you prove the baseline before they buy that.
